extracted.intended_audience: community program developers, nonprofit grant-seekers, and proposal writers (especially Illinois-based organizations)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, preparing, and writing project funding proposals for nonprofit/community programs, including pre-proposal research, strategy development, proposal components, budgeting, submission, and follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational mission alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Have clear and concise understanding of their purposes, missions, and goals; for the most part, do not attempt to develop and implement programs that are clearly outside the realm of their overall mission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders look for projects consistent with the organization's mission. Ensure the proposed project fits mission/strategic plans and explain why it belongs within your organization's scope. Avoid proposing programs that diverge from core mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic planning and program development
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage in systematic planning and program development activities; develop strategic plans for meeting short-range goals, realistically design and activate strategies for meeting long-term goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the project is part of deliberate strategic planning (not ad-hoc). Provide evidence of planning processes, timelines, and how the project advances short- and long-term goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background Information
rubrics_metrics.description: Who is the organization seeking funds, and what is its history? What qualifications show the organization can perform this program? What is the relationship of the organization's board of directors in the formation of policies? Was the board actively involved in the development of the project? Did the board approve the project and is it solidly committed to its implementation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concise organizational history, mission, track record, governance structure, and explicit statement that the board approved the project. Funders may check board awareness—include contactable references or documentation of board approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and Objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: What need is the organization seeking to meet? Is the problem to be addressed clearly defined? What is the proposed program? What are the specific objectives of the program, and what activities will be carried out to achieve the objectives? What is the project's timetable, and is it realistic?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State clear, specific, measurable objectives tied to activities and a realistic timeline. Objectives should flow logically from the needs assessment and be feasible within the proposed resources/time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Needs assessment / Problem statement
rubrics_metrics.description: The needs assessment or problem statement forms the basis for the development of the project and the request for project funding. A proposal is a written expression of, and proposed solution to, a problem. It must present a persuasive argument for the organization's case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a concise persuasive problem statement supported by documentation and empirical evidence. Use local data where possible; avoid inundating reviewers with raw statistics—interpret and link data to project rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of empirical data and source differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal reviewers welcome the use of documentation to support the claim or claims asserted in a needs assessment and problem statement. When presenting statistical information, remember that national statistics can be used for comparative and supportive purposes. There should always be differentiation between source data that is national in scope and data that is specific to the local area or community under study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite credible data sources (census, state agencies, university studies, local surveys). Distinguish national vs. local data and explain relevance to the target population. Use empirical methods appropriate to resources (surveys, intake logs, observation) and summarize findings rather than dumping raw tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data analysis and interpretation / comprehensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical studies provide an improved awareness of: types of needs and problems; severity of those needs; and who exhibits those needs. By comparing significant segments, or the same segment over time, the comparison should be able to allow for interpretations concerning which segments are affected the most, which segments are the largest, changes over time, and areas requiring action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze who is affected, how many, where they are, and severity. Use comparisons across segments or over time to justify priority. Consider producing a socioeconomic report or checklist covering demographics, income, service use, and service gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy identification and development
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the organization has determined what local situations need action and who and how people are affected, the organization would be ready to develop various strategies which can address the identified local problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generate multiple strategy options (brainstorm, review government/private models). Research existing government programs and private initiatives for applicable approaches. Document rationale for chosen strategy and how it adapts proven practices or innovates responsibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy feasibility and review
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze each suggested course of action in terms of its merit: available resources, constraints, methods to neutralize constraints, whether organization can carry it out, ability to obtain resources, potential blockers, client participation, duplication of services, consistency with organizational philosophy, cost versus expected results, and prior attempts by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically assess feasibility using the provided question set (e.g., 'Can our organization carry it out?', 'Would our clients participate?', 'Does this strategy duplicate other services?'). Document resource needs, mitigation of risks, and evidence of likely client uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting the proper funding agency (funder-fit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly described ideas directed in a timely manner to funding agencies with compatible interests are essential in obtaining a grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match project goals and target population to funder's mission and funding priorities. Research funders (government, corporations, foundations) and select those most likely to support your approach. Tailor language and emphasis to the funder's interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of deadlines is extremely important because many grants are awarded only once a year. Others may be rejected immediately simply because some of the required forms are missing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify application cycles, submission deadlines, and lead times. Schedule internal milestones to ensure completion of forms, attachments, and required approvals well before funder deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contacts, decision makers, and tracking contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify contacts/decision makers and track contacts. Proposal reviewers and funders have been known to call local or community contacts to check out an organization requesting funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a contact log of funder staff, reviewers, and local references. Make polite pre-proposal contacts where appropriate, and be prepared to provide verifiable local references who know the project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtaining local support and community involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain support from board members, project collaborators, clients, support agencies, and federal regional agency if applicable. Advance participation in planning by consumers and collaborators is important; many grant programs require sign-offs by relevant local organizations affected by the proposed project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure documented endorsements and evidence of community input/participation. Use local publicity and stakeholder meetings to build genuine support. Ensure letters or endorsements reflect real knowledge and commitment (not boilerplate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of letters of support
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters that are addressed to the agency director or board chairman and clearly reflect knowledge of the proposing organization, its work and track record, familiarity with proposed project, and pledge of assistance to the organization, should be included. Avoid vague or obviously solicited letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request specific letters that describe the author's relationship to the project, level of commitment, and how they will assist. Exclude generic or unsigned/unspecific statements that add no credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Getting expert advice / Technical assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Utilize the services of professionals whenever possible: fund raising consultants, state technical assistance staff, local professionals, educational institutions, Foundation Center resources, proposal writing seminars, and other technical assistance sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek outside review or consultation to strengthen proposal design, evaluation plans, and budgets. Use Foundation Center and local cooperating collections to research funders and application examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and compliance with required forms/certifications
rubrics_metrics.description: If special forms or certification are required, this should be determined in advance. Missing required forms can cause immediate rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a submission checklist to ensure all forms, signatures, attachments, certifications, and appendices are included and properly formatted. Confirm whether electronic or paper submission is required and follow instructions precisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal writing style and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful proposal writing is not complicated. It does, however, take a considerable amount of preparation and good organization. The grant-seeking organization should be clear in proposing what it will do. It should ask for resources which it obviously has a critical or pressing need to address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write clearly and concisely, avoid jargon, organize material logically, and integrate answers to common funder questions within the proposal body (especially when funders have no standard form). Emphasize what will be done, for whom, how, and why it matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover letter (component)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cover letter is a component of the proposal package and should appropriately accompany the submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the cover letter to succinctly introduce the project, state the amount requested, identify key contacts, and reference any attachments. Address it to the appropriate agency official and ensure an authorized signatory signs it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary / Executive summary (component)
rubrics_metrics.description: A summary should concisely present the proposed program, objectives, target population, timetable and funding request — the core information funders want answered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a short executive summary that can stand alone and quickly convey the project's purpose, scope, expected outcomes, total cost and request. Make it compelling and factual to engage reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology / Implementation plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the proposed program, activities to achieve objectives, staffing, management, and how the program will be implemented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete activity descriptions, responsible staff, timelines, recruitment/attendance plans, and any curriculum or service delivery details. Link activities directly to objectives and evaluation measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation plan
rubrics_metrics.description: What means will be employed to ensure that the stated needs and corresponding objectives are met? What provisions have been made to evaluate the program? Will project results be shared with others?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify measurable indicators, data collection methods, frequency, responsible parties, and how evaluation results will be used and disseminated. Include plans for formative and summative evaluation where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration and Management / Organizational capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: How is the organization going to implement and manage the program? Where does the project fit within the current management and organization structure? Is there adequate staffing or will additional or specialized staff be hired? What are the qualifications of key staff to be involved in the project?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline management structure, staff roles, hiring/training plans, and demonstrate staff qualifications and experience. Provide bios or resumes in the appendix for key personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget completeness and justification
rubrics_metrics.description: How much will the project cost in total, and how much is being requested of the funding agency? Typical line item costs and a well-structured budget are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a detailed line-item budget with clear justifications for each cost, a budget narrative tying costs to activities, and ensure consistency between budget and methodology. Use typical line items (personnel, fringe, equipment, supplies, travel, indirect) and explain unusual items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching share and in-kind contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Will the requesting organization contribute in-kind or cash to the project? Matching share concepts are emphasized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly state any cash or in-kind contributions, their valuation, and how they meet funder matching requirements. Document pledges or letters that verify commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cash flow and future funding / sustainability
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration should be given to the problem of continuing the project or service after the initial grant runs its course. What alternative sources of funding might pick up the program? Also plan for cash flow during the grant period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a plan for sustainability beyond the grant (future funding sources, phased-in revenue, institutionalization). Provide cash-flow projections if funder requires reimbursement-based payments and explain contingency plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendix and supporting materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements typically included in a proposal's appendix (e.g., letters of support, resumes, data tables, organizational documents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include only relevant supporting documents: board approval, resumes of key staff, MOUs, evaluation instruments, and specific data summaries. Avoid lengthy, unnecessary attachments; ensure all appendix items are referenced in the proposal body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding common grantseeking errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid common errors such as approaching incompatible funders, missing deadlines or required forms, submitting vague letters of support, lack of local/community buy-in, insufficient justification of need, and unrealistic budgets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the guide's checklists, have external reviewers proof the proposal, verify funder instructions, secure substantive local endorsements, and ensure budget/objectives/timeline consistency to reduce risk of immediate rejection.
